doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Teaching, history and the jazz tradition
title: The apprentice model versus jazz schools
summary: Thomas contrasts learning from masters in bands with codified school training, and notes that young players sound alike.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: See the way it used to be, it used to be in music that you learned by the old crafts model, the apprentice model. So as a beginner obviously you have to learn your craft, so you’re going to learn the basics in music. You’re going to learn how to play your instrument, how to play in tune if you’re playing a woodwind instrument like we do or like I did and you do. You’ve got your long tones, you’ve got to learn your scales in every key, you’ve got to learn your chords you know. You develop your own personal sound — at least you strive towards that. As a beginner usually that’s not the case because you don’t really have an instrumental identity yet. But along the way you play in bands, so it’s not just you playing in your room by yourself on your instrument and shedding with records, which is important. But you’ve got to play with other people. And through the process of playing with other people you start to grow, because you’re on that journey together and you see how to communicate, listen, respond to other people. But in playing with — the apprentice model had it where you would get with someone who is at another level and learn from them you know. And the ideal is when you get a chance to be with a master of the particular art form so that that master is, whether it’s verbally through, you know, when you’re practicing and they instruct you, or just more psychically you know. Because some leaders don’t really explain a lot you know. But you get it you know. And often times these masters are not just teaching about music. It’s about life. It’s about how you comport yourself as a young man or a woman in this field out here you know. That’s one of the things that anyone who’s going through that apprentice model, that’s what they tell you. They learned so much about life itself and relationships and such, not just

playing music though that’s primary. So you know you have a basic — you have the apprentice, you have a journeyman, you have you know craftsman and master craftsman. So when you go through that process you are developing yourself instrumentally, being able to play in a group context until you get to a point where you yourself say, are a master on your instrument, with your own voice, your own particular approach. Influenced — you’ve got those other people on the stage with you — but you still have your own identity, your own sound, your own particular approach that’s expressive of who you are. These days you have schools that have codified a particular way to learn how to play jazz. And so you have — and they serve their purpose. It’s important to have a codification of an art form when you have institutional structures through which people learn how to do things. Especially when you don’t have, first of all, the number of grand masters from the Golden Era less and less, that’s one thing. And you have less and less bands run by masters. There’s only a select number of slots in those bands you know. So when you had the big bands traveling, going on the road and you have bands in all these different venues, you had more opportunity for that. So there needs to be a way for a young person who wants to know how to play to do that. So that serves that purpose. But what has ended up happening in a lot of cases is that on a particular instrument you find a lot of the young players sound very similar. And you also find that they don’t seem to — let me learn the history, you know, chronological history of the music and that’s a necessary part of their study. They don’t necessarily seem to learn that history on the instrument. A lot of times you have artists who will start — if they start in the 50s that would be good. Because the 50s is the epicenter. You have all these different things. But a lot of times they start in the 60s. Or the 70s.
